name.text: C9.Q1 — The three-qubit bit-flip code, end to end

questiontext.text:
C9.Q1 — Encode, corrupt, diagnose, correct

\(\alpha|0\rangle+\beta|1\rangle\mapsto\alpha|000\rangle+\beta|111\rangle\), with syndrome \((Z_1Z_2, Z_2Z_3)\).

Write encode3(alpha, beta) returning the 8-dimensional encoded state; apply_x(state, q) applying \(X\) to qubit \(q\) (0 = most significant); syndrome3(state) returning the tuple of \(\pm1\) eigenvalues of \(Z_1Z_2\) and \(Z_2Z_3\) as ints; and correct3(state) returning the corrected state.

syndrome3(no error) -> (1, 1)
syndrome3(X on qubit 0) -> (-1, 1)
syndrome3(X on qubit 1) -> (-1, -1)
syndrome3(X on qubit 2) -> (1, -1)

testcode.text: import numpy as np v = encode3(0.6, 0.8) print(syndrome3(v))
import numpy as np v = encode3(0.6, 0.8) print([syndrome3(apply_x(v, q)) for q in range(3)])
import numpy as np v = encode3(0.6, 0.8) print(all(np.allclose(correct3(apply_x(v, q)), v) for q in range(3)))
import numpy as np v = encode3(1/np.sqrt(2), 1j/np.sqrt(2)) print(np.allclose(correct3(v), v))
import numpy as np v = encode3(0.6, 0.8) w = apply_x(apply_x(v, 0), 1) print(syndrome3(w), np.allclose(correct3(w), v))

name.text: C9.Q2 — Stabilizer codes in the symplectic representation

questiontext.text:
C9.Q2 — Syndromes as linear algebra over GF(2)

A Pauli on \(n\) qubits is a binary vector \((x|z)\); two Paulis commute iff \(x_1\!\cdot\!z_2+z_1\!\cdot\!x_2=0 \bmod 2\).

Write commutes(p1, p2, n) returning a bool; syndrome(error, stabilizers, n) returning a tuple of bits; is_valid_stabilizer_group(gens, n) checking that all generators pairwise commute; and weight(pauli, n) returning the number of qubits on which the Pauli acts non-trivially.

Steane code X-generators: IIIXXXX, IXXIIXX, XIXIXIX
and the mirrored Z-generators.

testcode.text: import numpy as np n=1 Xp=[1,0]; Zp=[0,1] print(commutes(Xp, Zp, n), commutes(Xp, Xp, n))

questiontext.text:
C9.Q3 — Is this code correcting?

\(P E_a^{\dagger}E_b P=c_{ab}P\) is necessary and sufficient. Checking it numerically for a small code is a direct matrix computation.

Write code_projector(basis) returning \(P=\sum_i |c_i\rangle\langle c_i|\) for an orthonormal list of codewords; and knill_laflamme(P, errors, tol=1e-9) returning True iff \(PE_a^{\dagger}E_bP\) is a scalar multiple of \(P\) for every pair.

3-qubit bit-flip code with errors {I, X1, X2, X3} -> True
same code with a Z error added                    -> False

testcode.text: import numpy as np c0 = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); c0[0] = 1 c1 = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); c1[7] = 1 P = code_projector([c0, c1]) print(np.allclose(P @ P, P), round(float(np.real(np.trace(P))), 6))

import numpy as np X = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]], dtype=complex); I2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex) def emb(U, q): ops = [I2]*3; ops[q] = U out = np.array([[1.0+0j]]) for o in ops: out = np.kron(out, o) return out c0 = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); c0[0] = 1 c1 = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); c1[7] = 1 P = code_projector([c0, c1]) errs = [np.eye(8, dtype=complex)] + [emb(X, q) for q in range(3)] print(knill_laflamme(P, errs))

import numpy as np X = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]], dtype=complex) Z = np.array([[1,0],[0,-1]], dtype=complex); I2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex) def emb(U, q): ops = [I2]*3; ops[q] = U out = np.array([[1.0+0j]]) for o in ops: out = np.kron(out, o) return out c0 = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); c0[0] = 1 c1 = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); c1[7] = 1 P = code_projector([c0, c1]) errs = [np.eye(8, dtype=complex)] + [emb(X, q) for q in range(3)] + [emb(Z, 0)] print(knill_laflamme(P, errs))

import numpy as np X = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]], dtype=complex); I2 = np.eye(2, dtype=complex) def emb(U, q): ops = [I2]*3; ops[q] = U out = np.array([[1.0+0j]]) for o in ops: out = np.kron(out, o) return out c0 = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); c0[0] = 1 c1 = np.zeros(8, dtype=complex); c1[7] = 1 P = code_projector([c0, c1]) errs = [np.eye(8, dtype=complex), emb(X, 0), emb(X, 1), emb(X, 2), emb(X,0) @ emb(X,1)] print(knill_laflamme(P, errs))
import numpy as np c0 = np.array([1, 0], dtype=complex) P = code_projector([c0]) print(knill_laflamme(P, [np.eye(2, dtype=complex)]))

questiontext.text:
C9.Q4 — When does error correction actually help?

A distance-\(d\) code suppresses errors as \(p_L\approx A(p/p_{\text{th}})^{\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor}\); concatenating \(\ell\) levels of a distance-3 code gives \(p_L\approx p_{\text{th}}(p/p_{\text{th}})^{2^{\ell}}\). Below threshold, more qubits help; above it, they hurt.

Write logical_error_surface(p, p_th, d, A=0.1); logical_error_concat(p, p_th, levels); and min_distance_for(p, p_th, target, A=0.1) returning the smallest odd \(d\ge3\) with logical_error_surface(p, p_th, d, A) <= target (search up to \(d=101\), return None if none works). Round the two error rates to 12 decimals.

logical_error_surface(1e-3, 1e-2, 3) -> 0.1 * (0.1)^2 = 0.001
min_distance_for(1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-12) -> 21

testcode.text: print(logical_error_surface(1e-3, 1e-2, 3))
print(min_distance_for(1e-3, 1e-2, 1e-12))
print(logical_error_concat(1e-3, 1e-2, 0), logical_error_concat(1e-3, 1e-2, 2))
print(min_distance_for(2e-2, 1e-2, 1e-12))
print(logical_error_surface(1e-3, 1e-2, 5) < logical_error_surface(1e-3, 1e-2, 3))
